bottleneck: Whether the adult human brain generates new neurons is still contested after decades: rodent hippocampal neurogenesis is robust, but human evidence relies on disputed markers in postmortem tissue, with landmark studies reaching opposite conclusions from similar samples. If human neurogenesis is negligible, regenerative strategies for the brain must come from transplantation or reprogramming rather than boosting endogenous growth; if it exists but declines with age, enhancing it could treat depression and dementia. The field cannot agree on the basic fact, so every downstream strategy rests on a disputed premise.
current_state: Single-cell sequencing and carbon-dating studies lean toward minimal adult human neurogenesis, but the debate is unresolved and methodologically fraught, with critics challenging each new method.

title: Adult human neurogenesis still contested
why_it_blocks: Brain repair strategies depend entirely on whether the brain can make new neurons. A foundational fact of human neurobiology remains an open argument — and billions in regenerative research are wagered on its outcome.
